findings.title: Write lock held during slow HTTP and filesystem I/O
findings.body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the potentially slow operations on lines 55-66: an HTTP request via readWebAssetsFromCDN and a filesystem read via readWebAssetsFromFile. Under concurrent requests with a cold cache, every caller will serialize on this single mutex. On a slow disk or CDN, this can cause request pile-up and latency spikes during the first requests after process start. The I/O should happen outside the critical section, with the lock held only for the pointer assignment, e.g. compute the result first, then Lock() briefly to install it.

findings.title: Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent cold-cache callers all redo the I/O
findings.body: The pattern takes RLock, snapshots the pointer, releases RLock, checks for nil, then takes Lock. After acquiring Lock, the cache is never re-checked. So if N goroutines all observe a nil cache under RLock, they all proceed to perform the file/CDN read in series (since the Lock from line 48 also serializes them) and each overwrites entryPointAssetsCache with its own result. This is functionally correct but wastes I/O and means the first N callers all pay the full initialization cost. Re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and early-return if populated, or use sync.Once to gate the load so only the first caller does the work.

findings.title: Cached pointer is shared with all callers; lock only protects the slot, not the contents
findings.body: The mutex added in this PR only guards the entryPointAssetsCache variable itself. The function returns that exact pointer on every call (line 70), so every caller receives the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets instance, including its JSFiles slice header. Any caller that mutates the returned object (e.g. appending to JSFiles or relying on a copy-on-write assumption) will race against every other concurrent reader and against future cache reads. The PR description says it fixes a data race, but this remaining aliasing is a latent source of the same class of bug; consider returning a copy or documenting the aliasing contract.
